## Objectives

- Run the k-means algorithm by hand once, so it is never a black box again
- Understand what it minimises, and why that makes it fast and fallible
- Choose $k$ with a method you can defend to a colleague
- Turn clusters into **segments**: profiles a marketing team, or a care manager, can use

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
One plan for everyone, or one for each person? Neither.
:::

| | One for everyone | One for each | The compromise |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Retailer** | mass marketing, paid for people who never respond | one-to-one, for 400 000 customers | **segments**: a few offers |
| **Health authority** | one pathway, for an average patient nobody is | one plan each, for 400 000 residents | **patient groups**: a few pathways |

: {tbl-colwidths="[19,33,26,22]"}

- Every CRM has a segmentation inside — usually a k-means, run once in 2019 and never revisited
- Population health management groups patients the same way: healthy, chronic, complex and frail

By the end of today you can build one, and you know what is wrong with the one you inherit.

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} The algorithm {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## What k-means wants

Given $n$ points and a number $k$ that **you** choose, find $k$ groups $C_1,\dots,C_k$ that minimise the **within-cluster sum of squares**:

$$
W(C) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k} \;\sum_{i \in C_j} \lVert x_i - \bar{x}_j \rVert^2
$$

- $\bar x_j$ is the **centroid** of cluster $j$: the mean of its points
- Small $W$: every point close to its own centroid — ANOVA's within-group variance

::: {.callout-note}
The true minimum is out of reach: 100 customers split into 3 groups about $10^{47}$ ways, into 10 about $10^{93}$ — more than the atoms in the universe. k-means finds a *good* one, fast.
:::

## Lloyd's algorithm, four lines

1. Pick $k$ points at random as initial centroids
2. **Assign** each point to the nearest centroid
3. **Update** each centroid to the mean of its assigned points
4. Repeat 2–3 until nothing moves

Each step can only lower $W$, so it always stops. Usually within a dozen rounds.

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
It stops at *a* minimum, not *the* minimum. Different starting points give different answers. Always run it several times and keep the best: `nstart = 25`, never `nstart = 1`.
:::

## Assign, update, repeat

{{< video media/Lloyd.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

66 customers, bad starting centroids on purpose. Watch the column of $W$: it only falls, which is *why* the algorithm has to stop.

## By hand: six customers, two variables

::: {.subtitle-frame}
How often they come, and how much they spend each time · both on a 0–10 score
:::

| | A | B | C | D | E | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| visits per month | 1 | 2 | 1 | 8 | 9 | 8 |
| spend per visit | 1 | 1 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 9 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[28,12,12,12,12,12,12]"}

$k = 2$, starting centres **A** and **D**.

1. **Assign**: every customer joins the nearer centre. B and C are close to A; E and F close to D
2. **Update**: each centre moves to the average of its group: $(1.33, 1.33)$ and $(8.33, 8.33)$
3. **Assign again**: nobody changes group, so it stops. One round was enough

$W$ adds up each customer's squared distance from its centre: $\tfrac{8}{3} \approx 2.67$. Any other split of the six gives more.

## By hand, watched

{{< video media/KmeansByHand.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

Every squared distance, both centroid updates, and $W$ at the end. Six points is small enough to check the algorithm's arithmetic against your own.

## Two things that silently break it

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Both happen in every real dataset
:::

**Scale.** Cost of care in euros and age in years: cost dominates the distance entirely, age is noise. k-means sees only geometry. **Standardise first** — `scale()` — unless you have a reason not to.

**Shape.** k-means draws straight boundaries between centroids. It finds round, similar-sized blobs. Give it two crescents, or one dense core inside a diffuse halo, and it will cut them wrongly and report a fine $W$.

::: {.callout-note}
Neither failure produces an error message. The output looks like any other segmentation. This is why you *look at the plot* before you trust the numbers.
:::

## Scale: the distance is cost

{{< video media/ScaleBreaks.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

$37^2 = 1\,369$ against $600^2 = 360\,000$: age is 0.4% of the distance. The clusters are cost bands, young and old mixed in both — until `scale()`.

## Shape: the failure with no error message

{{< video media/ShapeBreaks.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

Two crescents any eye separates. k-means cuts them with a straight line, and that cut has *less than half* the $W$ of the true groups: more starts cannot help.

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Choosing k {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## $W$ always falls as $k$ grows

- $k = 1$: $W$ is the total variance
- $k = n$: $W = 0$, every point is its own cluster
- In between, $W$ falls monotonically. It **cannot** choose $k$ for you — it always votes for more.

## The elbow, and the elbow you actually get

{{< video media/ElbowLie.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

Textbook curves have a corner. Most real ones bend smoothly, and the elbow you *find* is the elbow you went looking for.

## Two honest tools

- **Elbow**: plot $W$ against $k$; take $k$ where the curve stops bending. Crude, quick, often enough.
- **Silhouette**: for each point, *how much closer is it to its own cluster than to the next one?* Average it; pick the $k$ that maximises. Ranges $-1$ to $1$; above $0.5$ is a real structure, below $0.25$ is not.

When they disagree, bring a third: stability across seeds, or how many segments a team can actually act on.

## The silhouette, watched

{{< video media/Silhouette.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

The customer nearest a border: $a = 2.54$, $b = 3.65$, $s = 0.30$. The average over all 66 is 0.66 at $k = 3$, against 0.50, 0.56, 0.47, 0.36 for $k = 2, 4, 5, 6$: pick three.

## In R

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7-8|10"}
library(tidyverse); library(factoextra)
X <- scale(USArrests)                      # always: same units for every column

fviz_nbclust(X, kmeans, method = "wss")    # elbow
fviz_nbclust(X, kmeans, method = "silhouette")

set.seed(1)
km <- kmeans(X, centers = 4, nstart = 25)  # 25 random starts, keep the best

fviz_cluster(km, data = X)                 # the picture you show a colleague
```

::: {.callout-note}
`set.seed()` makes the random starts reproducible. Without it, your colleague reruns your script and gets different segment numbers — the same segments, relabelled — and a meeting is lost to confusion.
:::

## [Drill 1]{.drill-kicker} Pick $k$, and say why

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · what the block above gives on `USArrests`
:::

| $k$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $W$ | 196.0 | 102.9 | 78.3 | 56.4 | 48.9 | 42.8 | 38.3 | 34.4 |
| Silhouette | — | 0.41 | 0.31 | 0.34 | 0.30 | 0.29 | 0.29 | 0.26 |

1. Which $k$ does the elbow suggest? And the silhouette?
2. Which $k$ do you take to your manager? Write the **one sentence** you say when they ask why.

## [Drill 1 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Two criteria, one decision

- **Elbow**: $W$ falls by 93, then 25, 22, then 7.5 — the curve stops bending after $k = 4$
- **Silhouette**: best at $k = 2$ (0.41), second best at $k = 4$ (0.34). Nothing reaches 0.5: the structure is moderate, not sharp
- $k = 2$ is *high crime against low crime*: true, and no news. $k = 4$ also splits urban from rural states, and the same four groups come back from every seed tried

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"Four: the gain in $W$ collapses after four, the silhouette's second peak is at four, and only four groups separate the rural states with the most murders from the urban ones with the most assaults."
:::

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} From clusters to segments {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## A cluster is a set of rows. A segment is a story.

The algorithm gives you `1, 2, 3, 4`. Nobody in marketing can act on `3`.

**Profile** each cluster: the mean of every variable, per cluster, back in the original units.

| Segment | Visits / month | Spend per visit (€) | Tenure (yrs) | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.8 | 62 | 1.1 | 41% |
| 2 | 6.4 | 28 | 4.8 | 22% |
| 3 | 2.1 | 140 | 3.9 | 19% |
| 4 | 4.0 | 55 | 0.4 | 18% |

Then **name** them from the numbers — *occasional big spenders*, *frequent small spenders*, … — and only then hand them over.

## What "act on it" looks like

- **Segment 1** · *the quiet majority* (0.8 visits, 1.1 years, 41%): the biggest group and the least attached — give them a reason to come back, not a bigger bill
- **Segment 2** · *loyalists* (6.4 visits, €28): cross-sell, not discount — they already come; raise what they spend
- **Segment 3** · *big spenders* (€140, 2.1 visits): the opposite — they spend when they come; one more visit a quarter beats any upsell
- **Segment 4** · *new regulars* (0.4 years, 4 visits): the retention window is now; a churn model (week 4) will tell you *which* of them

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
The segmentation is only as good as the variables you fed it. Cluster on demographics and you get demographic segments, which rarely predict behaviour. Cluster on **behaviour** — recency, frequency, monetary value — and the segments are things a company can move.
:::

## [Drill 2]{.drill-kicker} Now the patients

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · a health district, $k = 4$ on scaled columns · means per patient, per year
:::

| Group | Age | Conditions | ED visits | Admissions | Cost (€) | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 34 | 0.2 | 0.3 | 0.02 | 310 | 58% |
| 2 | 67 | 2.1 | 0.6 | 0.10 | 2 400 | 27% |
| 3 | 81 | 4.3 | 2.8 | 1.30 | 14 800 | 6% |
| 4 | 45 | 1.0 | 4.1 | 0.15 | 1 900 | 9% |

1. A **name** for each group, from the numbers — one a care manager would use
2. Which group gets a case manager first? Back it with **one number computed** from the table
3. Group 4 visits the emergency department (ED) four times a year and is rarely admitted. Why, and what would you change?

## [Drill 2 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Four groups, four pathways

- **1 · healthy, low users** (34 years, €310): prevention and screening, nothing more
- **2 · chronic and stable** (2.1 conditions, rarely admitted): a disease pathway run by the GP — diabetes, heart failure
- **3 · complex and frail** (81 years, 1.3 admissions): **6% of patients, 47% of the spending** — case management and care at home, to prevent the next admission
- **4 · the ED as their GP** (4.1 visits, 0.15 admissions): not sick enough to stay, so not an emergency — open primary care in the evening, not more beds

[Per 100 patients: $6 \times 14\,800 = 88\,800$ out of $58 \times 310 + 27 \times 2\,400 + 6 \times 14\,800 + 9 \times 1\,900 = 188\,680$ euro.]{.muted}

## k-means answers "how many groups?" with "as many as you asked for." {.statement}

[The choice of $k$ is a decision, and it is yours.]{.muted}
